# 01 â€” Framing brief: a `browser` engine for the reviewer bridge (web-chat reviewers via the user's own Chrome tab)

**Context.** The bridge (this repo = the PowerShell plugin; `C:\Users\Dmytro\C3` = its Rust port with engines codex / agy /
muse / claude / http and a "reviewer pack" for models without repository tools) lets a coordinator consult reviewers
from different labs. Many labs answer only in the browser: for free (grok.com) or under a chat subscription the user
already has (Gemini web with a Pro plan â†’ gemini-3.8-flash) but no API/CLI plan. The operator wants a `browser` engine:
the bridge drives a web chat UI through Chrome, so a roster can hold `browser :: gemini-web`, `browser :: grok`.

**Hard boundary set by the operator (read this first).** Automating a vendor's web chat sits in a grey zone of the
vendors' terms. Therefore the PRODUCT must stay a neutral frame: engine, adapter contract, sandbox, telemetry fields,
catalogue format, signing. SITE ADAPTERS (the DOM logic for a given site) are user-land: written, enabled and run by the
user in the user's own signed-in browser session. We ship no adapter for a site whose terms forbid automation; the
operator wants the company clearly outside the grey area. Please treat this as a design constraint, not as a question.

**Prior art (same author, reusable).** `C:\Users\Dmytro\gemini-mcp` (read `DESIGN.md` Â§"Transport: an in-tab extension
relay", Â§"WebSocket message contract", Â§"Security stance"; `PROTOCOL.md` explains why cookie/HTTP replay was abandoned):
a Chrome extension + local WebSocket relay that gives the Gemini web app MCP tools; no API key, no cookies, the signed-in
tab is the credential. `C:\Users\Dmytro\xelth.rs` README "Chrome Extension: DOM Heuristic Doctor" (retry loops, fuzzy
selectors, status badge). ROADMAP section "Browser engine" in this repo (just added) sketches the shape: C3 â†” local WS â†”
extension â†” adapter (WASM in the extension, contract `new_chat / send / await_answer / attach? / limits`), reviewer pack
as the only input (no repo tools), verbatim reply â†’ the usual ledger/findings/ratings, telemetry fields
`adapter_id/version/site`, adapters rated and distributed through the usefulness channel with signatures (xelixir
"WASM shield" rule: user-installed, lands disabled, enabled explicitly).

**Questions (answer by number, â‰¤700 words, concrete):**
- Q1. Boundary design: what must the product NOT contain (code, defaults, docs, catalogue entries) so that it is plainly
  a neutral automation frame and the adapter author carries the site-terms responsibility? Precedents you know
  (browser extensions, userscript managers, OpenInterpreter-style tools, "bring your own session" products) and how they

- Q2. Technical shape: WASM adapters inside the extension (host API = DOM read/click/type on the chat tab only) vs.

  exposure, no cross-tab reach), most robust to DOM churn, and simplest to sandbox and sign? What is the minimal
  adapter contract that covers Gemini web, grok.com, and a generic "textarea + answer container" site?
- Q3. Detection/abuse: how to keep the engine on the right side â€” human cadence, user-visible turns, per-adapter rate

- Q4. Reviewer quality: a web reviewer gets only the pack text (small free-tier contexts). Pack budget per adapter, how

- Q5. Telemetry/distribution: which fields per consultation (adapter id/version, site, outcome class) and what the

- Q6. Order of work and what you would NOT build. Blockers vs. fix-after.

# Roadmap

Features the bridge should grow. Each entry names the problem it solves; the order is the
order we would build them. Released so far: 0.2.0, 0.3.0, 0.4.0 (2026-09-26) 0.5.0 (2026-09-30: R12, R14-R20, R23; hosts Claude Code, Codex CLI, Z Code, Kimi Code) and 0.6.0 (2026-10-08: R10's claude engine with its endpoint mode, wave 28e, the roster value panel: light). Next: R8/R9. Agreed on 2026-09-23 between the Claude Code coordinator and the
Codex reviewer after a seven-wave implementation task with three consultations (framing,
acceptance, re-acceptance), and merged with the earlier help-wanted list.

## Review workflow

- **R1 â€” Core-contract checkpoint preset.** A review mode meant to run BEFORE dependent
  implementation starts (once the core interfaces, recovery and persistence paths exist) and to
  be re-triggered by changes to recovery, persistence or interfaces. Rationale: on the task that
  motivated this list every acceptance HOLD cost a full fix wave, because the core had been
  built on and the state-machine defects were found only at the end. Reviewing every mechanical
  wave is not the answer; reviewing contract boundaries is.
  **Status (0.2.0): shipped** â€” `-Purpose core-contract` (xhigh effort, 900-word preset),
  narrowed by amendment to the interfaces and state machines named in the brief rather than
  the whole system, to fit the word budget.
- **R2 â€” Brief template.** A skeleton the coordinator fills for a checkpoint or acceptance:
  delta since the last review, the invariants claimed, changed files, unresolved findings,
  evidence paths, and the decision requested. Small critical executable files (a boot hook, an
  install script) go inline; everything else by exact path and revision. Rationale: a spec-only
  brief hid a one-character glob bug in a 100-line hook that a code reader would have seen.
  **Status (0.2.0): shipped** â€” `templates/brief-framing.md` and `templates/brief-review.md`.
- **R3 â€” Structured findings companion.** Beside the Markdown reply, a machine-readable list
  (via Codex `--output-schema`, already on the help-wanted list): finding id, severity,
  file:line, claim, trigger, evidence level, verification step, proposed remedy. Rationale: the
  coordinator verifies every finding before acting; a parseable list makes that step and the
  later "verified" bookkeeping (see TECH_DEBT T1) mechanical. Structure is not proof; the
  verification step stays.
  **Status (0.2.0): shipped**, revised beyond the original proposal after a design-review
  HOLD: `evidence` became an array of `{kind, reference, observation}` (what was already
  checked, not just a level), `locations[]` replaced a `"path:line"` string, and every reply
  is locally validated against the schema (see TECH_DEBT T1 status).
- **R4 â€” Acceptance output standard.** Every acceptance reply ends with four fixed blocks:
  verdict, blockers, unproven scenarios, and an OBSERVABLE first-run checklist (what must be
  in the logs before an exit code 0 is believed). Rationale: "what would justify acceptance?"
  was the most useful thing the reviewer produced, and it should not depend on being asked.
  **Status (0.2.0): shipped** â€” the four blocks are rendered LAST in the reply file (after
  the verbatim prose, findings and prior findings), per the design-review amendment.
- **R5 â€” Review-purpose presets with measurements.** Presets for framing / checkpoint /
  acceptance / diff review with default effort levels, and a ledger record of effort, latency
  and the rework each review triggered. Rationale: a medium-effort checkpoint may be the right
  trade for quota, but today there is no comparison that proves it; measure first.
  **Status (0.2.0): shipped** â€” the preset table plus `codex-findings.ps1 -Stats`, joining
  findings to the consultation that produced them via `source.consult`.
- **R6 â€” Role-split guidance.** Document primary (not exclusive) responsibilities when two
  reviewers exist: a fresh-context verifier of the same model family for mechanics (lint,
  interpreter compatibility, build, test wiring) and the Codex reviewer for protocol, state
  machines and "what the evidence does not show". Either may challenge anything. Rationale: on
  the motivating task the two found mostly different defects; together they were the coverage.
  **Status (0.2.0): shipped** â€” a "Role split" section in the skill and the README; no
  tooling enforces it, it is guidance for the coordinator.

## Additional reviewers (planned for 0.3.0)

Agreed on 2026-09-23 from one brief answered independently by the Codex reviewer and by
GLM-5.3 (`.collab/multi-model-2026-09-23/`). Facts that shaped it: Codex CLI runs GLM-5.3 as
its model through the z.ai devpack provider (`-c model_provider=ZAI -m glm-5.3`) and the bridge
already works that way end to end; `--output-schema` is NOT enforced server-side on that route
(the reply came back as a fenced JSON block, field-complete, which the 0.2.0 parser accepts and
validates locally); a Codex thread cannot be resumed under another provider once it holds
OpenAI compaction items. Both reviewers agreed that an additional model is a measured,
optional participant whose "done" is never trusted and who never closes a finding.

- **R7 â€” Provider support with reviewer lineages.** `-Provider <name>` on the bridge (a
  `model_providers` entry from the user's Codex config), with every thread bound to
  provider + model + harness (+ a config fingerprint); the parent thread for `fork`/`resume`
  chosen from the latest thread WITHIN that lineage, never the task's latest thread globally;
  fork/resume across lineages refused; the resolved model recorded instead of "config default";
  per-provider effort mapping (Codex `low|medium|high|xhigh`, GLM `low|high|max`) with requested
  and effective values in the ledger; a provider allowlist; a peak-hour warning with optional
  off-peak-only enforcement and per-consult credit estimates (the tariff calendar is not
  hard-coded â€” it changes). Only supported-tool routes (Codex CLI, Claude Code) ever carry plan
  credentials; the bridge never makes a direct HTTP call. Until R7 exists, a second model is
  consulted through the Claude Code worker wire and its reply saved as a handoff by hand.
  **Status (0.3.0): shipped**, after a design-review round
  (`.collab/bridge-0.3-2026-09-24/`, findings `F02-1`..`F02-9`) that amended the design
  before implementation: provider identity is read from the Codex config (or given
  explicitly) rather than assumed `openai`, via a constrained TOML scanner that refuses
  (naming the line) any construct it does not understand rather than guessing; the
  compatibility identity gating `fork`/`resume` across a lineage is narrowed to
  `base_url` + `wire_api` only (a canonicalised fingerprint), so comments, key order and
  secret rotation never break a lineage while an endpoint or protocol change does; a
  per-run `consult_id` in the prompt makes the rollout-file thread fallback verified
  rather than a best guess (an unverified candidate is kept only as a diagnostic, never
  as a parent); effort vocabularies are keyed by the provider's endpoint host (with
  no model-prefix fallback since F02-4: only models declared for the host) instead of by alias, `-NativeEffort` as the escape hatch, and
  `effort_requested`/`effort_sent`/`effort_mapping`/`effort_confirmed` (the last always
  `null` â€” not observable) replace a single `-Effort` value; peak-hour handling got exact
  semantics (fixed offset, inclusive start/exclusive end, overnight windows, exception
  dates; checked early and again immediately before launch - the launch-time result governs) and `-OffPeakOnly` refuses on an unknown schedule as well as
  on peak. Legacy (pre-0.3.0) ledger entries are unknown provenance and are never
  automatic parents â€” the first 0.3.0 consultation on an old task always starts a new
  thread. Not adopted: per-consult credit estimates (the tariff calendar is not
  hard-coded and estimating it well is its own project) and a provider allowlist beyond
  "must be a table the scanner can read".
- **R8 â€” Requested checks.** A reviewer may list `requested_checks[]`: one command or
  procedure + expected observation each, tied to a finding or invariant, capped per brief; the
  coordinator chooses the executor (a cheaper model or a worker) and records completion
  separately with revision, log, exit status and observed result. `unproven[]` keeps the
  uncertainty, `requested_checks[]` says how to resolve it. First a brief/reply convention,
  then a schema field once it has been used a few times.
  **Status (0.3.0): shipped as a convention, not a schema field** â€” the structured-mode
  prompt asks Codex to end `reply_markdown` with a `## Requested checks` section
  (`RC1..RCn`, at most 5, each one command/procedure with cwd, permission, expected
  observation and budget) when it has evidence it cannot obtain read-only; the schema
  stays v1 and the bridge renders nothing extra. `templates/brief-review.md` gained a
  "Requested checks run" table for the coordinator to fill in the next brief. A schema
  field remains for later, once the convention has real usage to generalise from.
- **R9 â€” Review groups for fan-out.** One revision-bound brief to two reviewers in fresh
  threads, neither seeing the other's answer first, at contract boundaries and acceptance only.
  Their findings keep separate ids; the coordinator links them to a canonical issue with
  `corroborates` / `contradicts` / `duplicates` under a review-group id. Agreement prioritises
  investigation and may lighten a spot-check; it never replaces verification. Measured by
  unique verified defects, false positives, coordinator verification minutes and avoided
  rework; routine fan-out stops when the margin is poor.
  **Status: partially shipped in 0.3.0, the rest deferred to 0.4.0.** The reviewer
  roster (`CODEX_CONSULT_ROSTER`, an ordered list of reviewers with credential/panel
  metadata) and the review **panel** (`-Panel`/`-PanelAll`: the same brief sent to every
  available roster entry, sequentially, each its own consultation in its own lineage,
  own reply file and own ledger `panel` record) shipped, along with the per-reviewer
  **scoreboard** (`codex-findings.ps1 -Stats`: raised/verified/implemented/proposed/
  rejected/wontfix/superseded per lineage) â€” see the README's "Reviewer roster and
  panel" section. What did NOT ship, and stays deferred to 0.4.0
  (`.collab/bridge-0.3-2026-09-24/state.md`; findings `F02-6`/`F02-7`/`F02-8` recorded
  `wontfix` in the 0.3.0 task with a pointer here): the panel is explicitly **NOT blind
  between waves** â€” every member of one panel run sees the same open-findings snapshot
  taken when the panel started, which is a real improvement over ad hoc sequential
  fan-out, but a later panel on the same task still sees the earlier panel's findings,
  so cross-wave independence still does not exist; there is still no `corroborates`/
  `contradicts`/`duplicates` relation tooling (`-Link`), no canonical-issue id, and no
  grouped stats beyond the per-lineage scoreboard. Before that ships it still needs: an
  immutable group manifest (brief hash, source/artifact fingerprints, purpose, shared
  instructions, frozen baseline findings, member attempts); genuine blind baseline
  isolation across waves; canonical-issue membership and report-validity adjudication
  kept distinct from fix status; verification-time records; nullable avoided-rework
  estimates; idempotent atomic relations (`-Link` must not create duplicate or
  asymmetric edges on a retry); and failed attempts recorded, not only successful ones.
- **R10 â€” Engines: each provider through its own official protocol (planned for 0.4.0).**
  Today every reviewer is reached through `codex exec`, whose only structured-output path is
  the Responses API `json_schema` response format â€” ignored by some third-party endpoints and
  rejected by others, which is why 0.3.0 needed the contract-first prompt and the one
  format-repair turn. The same models answer with native structured output when consulted
  through the CLI their provider officially supports: Claude Code headless
  (`claude -p --json-schema <schema> --output-format json`, an Anthropic-compatible endpoint
  in the child process only; `--resume`/`--fork-session` for lineage) and Google's
  Antigravity CLI (`agy -p --json-schema ... --output-format json`, `--conversation <id>`),
  which share one flag surface â€” verified live on 2026-09-25 with a GLM route, a MiMo route
  and a Gemini model, each returning `structured_output` on the first turn. R10 adds a roster
  field `engine` = `codex` (default) | `claude` | `agy`, one headless adapter for the
  Claude-Code-style CLIs (argv, JSON envelope, session id as the thread, usage), the same
  ledger, findings, panel, scoreboard and preflight (credential = the CLI's own login or the
  endpoint's env key; a CLI that reports `authentication required` is `unavailable`), and
  caps-v1 entries per engine (effort vocabulary, schema transport `native`). Non-goals: any
  direct HTTP client with a subscription key (the plans forbid it), a gateway/proxy between
  Codex and a provider, and mixing engines inside one lineage (a thread belongs to one
  engine as it belongs to one provider). Measured by first-turn structured rate per route
  and by the scoreboard's hit rate per (engine, provider, purpose).
  **Status: `agy` shipped (0.4.0, wave 17); `claude` shipped (0.6.0, waves 29 and 29b - the Claude subscription, an API key or a third-party Anthropic-compatible endpoint; decisions D1-D12, E1-E17, A1-A6 in `.collab/claude-engine-2026-09-30/`).** The engine table
  (`$script:Engines`) with its first row `agy` - after a design round with a panel (GLM,
  MiMo) and Gemini itself (`.collab/engines-0.4-2026-09-25/`), whose amendments A1-A20 are in
  the code: stdin stream-json transport (one NDJSON line), default mode `new`, the
  conversation-id rules (a resume, repair or retry that lands in another conversation
  fails), exactly one `result` event, the F11 denial retry, the `permission` failure class
  and Google's error/retry wordings, `agy models` as the sign-in check (never in the hook),
  and - because agy's `--sandbox` does not block writes (F12) - the bridge's tree check
  failing any agy run that changed the working tree or (wave 18) anything in the collab
  directory; wave 18 also records the retry turns' event streams in the ledger, rejects
  trailing garbage after exit 0, warns on a non-unique `-Provider` label and gives the
  sign-in check 45 s plus a ledger short-circuit (a usable agy reply within 60 minutes).
  Gitignored paths, submodules and files outside the repository stay unmonitored. The `claude`
  engine is the next row of the same table (argv, stdin, event parser, turn rules,
  credential) without touching the run block again. Open: TECH_DEBT T7 (an agy lineage binds
  engine + label + model, not the signed-in account).
- **R11 â€” Parallel panel (0.4.x wave 21 - implemented in the 0.4.0 candidate; first live run
  2026-09-26: 8 members, at most 7 at a time, 30 min wall clock against about 107 min summed).** A `-Panel` run consults its
  members one after another (README, "Reviewer roster and panel"), so its wall clock is the
  SUM of the members' times (a two-member framing panel today: 8-12 minutes). The members are
  already independent â€” each gets the same brief and the same snapshot of the findings that
  were open when the panel started, never another member's reply â€” so nothing in the review
  itself needs the order; what forces it is the machinery: one task lock (`.consult.lock`)
  and one recovery record per task, the ledger appended under that lock, handoff numbers
  taken at each member's start, and a survivor scan that looks for codex-like processes by
  NAME and would take a sibling member's process for an orphan. R11 runs the members
  concurrently: a panel-level lock that owns the task for the whole panel, `n` and `NN`
  assigned to every member when the panel starts (so the files and ledger entries keep the
  roster order whatever finishes first), one recovery record per member (`.consult.pending-
  <member>.json`, the recovery path checks all of them), the survivor scan by the recorded
  pid + start time only, and one summary written after the last member. Invariants kept: the
  members stay blind to each other inside a wave; the same open-findings snapshot; exit 0
  only when every member produced a usable reply; nothing already written is lost when one
  member dies. The agy engine's collab-root snapshot (0.4.0, wave 18) must then exclude the
  sibling members' own files, or every concurrent member would fail the others' tree check. Non-goals: concurrent consultations OUTSIDE a panel (two `-Panel` runs or a
  single run beside a panel on one task are still refused by the lock), and any change to
  what a member sees. Measured by the panel's wall clock (max of the members instead of
  their sum) and by an unchanged per-member result set against the sequential harness cases.
  **Status (wave 21, fakes only):** built per the design round
  `.collab/parallel-panel-2026-09-25/` (decisions D1-D13): members in parallel across
  endpoints (one after another within one; roster `"parallel"`, `-PanelConcurrency`), the
  panel run holding the task lock, n/NN and one `reserved` record per member up front,
  the member's proof of its parent, writer liveness for every record, the commit write lock
  with re-read and own delta (single runs and `codex-findings.ps1` too), `finished_at` for
  endpoint health; `tests/harness-panel.ps1`. Next: a live parallel panel reviews the wave.
- **R12 â€” Non-blocking consultation (planned for 0.4.x, with or after R11).** Today a
  consultation or a panel holds the coordinator's turn until the last reply is in (a
  two-member framing panel: 8-12 minutes; three members: 20+). The coordinator should be
  able to put a question to the panel, go on with other work, and come back to THAT question
  when the panel has finished. Pieces: a `-Detach` switch that validates, locks and
  launches exactly as today but returns immediately with the panel id and the path of a
  status file (`<task>/.panel-<id>.status.json`: members, state per member, the summary
  once written) instead of waiting; a `codex-panel.ps1 -Status <id>` (or
  `codex-findings.ps1 -List`) that prints the state and, when done, the same summary block a
  blocking run prints; the reservation and recovery record unchanged, so a detached run that
  dies is recovered like any other; a note in the consult-codex skill telling the coordinator
  how to park the question (the brief's path and the panel id in `state.md`) and when to
  revisit it (never before every member is `usable` or `failed`). Non-goals: a daemon, a
  queue of consultations, notifications through anything but the status file and the
  hooks a host already runs (a SessionStart/Stop hook may print "panel <id> finished").
  Measured by the coordinator's blocked time per consultation (from the panel's wall clock
  to seconds) with unchanged ledger, findings and recovery semantics.
- **R13 â€” Host invariance: the same bridge for a Codex-first (or any) coordinator (implemented in the 0.5.0 candidate, wave 27 and 27b - hosts Claude Code, Codex CLI, Z Code, Kimi Code, any shell;
  the live coordinator runs are listed in README "Tested on").** The bridge scripts already run from any coordinator - a Codex CLI session, Cursor,
  a shell - and a reviewer needs no ChatGPT plan (a provider table with an `env_key`
  authenticates on its own; the preflight checks `codex login status` only for `openai`).
  What is Claude-Code-specific is the packaging: the `.claude-plugin` manifest, `hooks.json`,
  `claude plugin eval`, the `${CLAUDE_PLUGIN_ROOT}` paths inside the two skills, and wording
  that names Claude as the judge. R13 makes the host a parameter: (a) the skills reference
  the bridge through one documented root variable with a plain-path fallback, so the same
  SKILL.md files (they already follow the open Agent Skills format) install into
  `~/.codex/skills`, Cursor or any host that reads SKILL.md; (b) an `install.ps1` that copies
  the skills and prints the host-specific lines (Claude Code: enable the plugin; Codex: an
  AGENTS.md snippet with the one command and the process; others: the SKILL.md path); (c)
  the council text says "the coordinator" where it says "Claude" - the judge is whoever runs
  the bridge, and the roster must then avoid consulting the coordinator's own model as a
  reviewer (a lineage equal to the coordinator's model is a warning); (d) the SessionStart
  availability line for hosts without hooks becomes a documented one-liner
  (`codex-consult-hook.ps1`) the coordinator runs at the start of a session. Non-goals: a
  second packaging format per host, a rename of the plugin or marketplace ids (installed
  copies key on them); the short name **CCC** (Claude Codex Consult) is used in the docs until
  1.0.0, which will be released under the name **C3** (the same three words, and a nod to a
  certain protocol droid that translates between parties and never stops advising) - the
  plugin and marketplace ids change only then, with a migration note for installed copies.
  Measured by one fresh Codex-CLI-coordinated consultation from the README alone.
- **R14 â€” Adaptive companions: panel size and diversity follow the stakes (implemented in the 0.5.0
  candidate, wave 26, f29f5ca, with R15 and R16; the acceptance panel of 2026-09-27 - the first live
  routed panel - held on one major, fixed in wave 26b together with R18/R20 below).**
  The coordinator never takes a non-trivial step alone, and a panel grows with the stakes instead of
  always taking every available reviewer. This project's own evidence: in the R11 design review
  (`.collab/parallel-panel-2026-09-25/`, three reviewers from three labs) the most serious hole - a
  member's recovery record reading inactive while it commits - was found independently by all three,
  and each of them also found something the other two missed (atomic-write temp files; endpoint
  health ordering and per-endpoint concurrency; commits of other tasks failing an agy member).
  Pieces: (a) a default panel size per purpose (checkpoint 1; framing and decision 2-3;
  core-contract and acceptance 3-5; stuck: every available reviewer), overridable with
  `-PanelSize <n>`; (b) diversity first: members from different labs before a second model of one
  lab (an optional roster field `lab`, defaulting to the provider label); (c) a floor of one
  companion on framing and decision, so a design is never reviewed only by its author - the
  consult-codex skill states it as a rule; (d) diminishing returns documented: past about five
  diverse members, extra reviewers mostly repeat findings while costing quota and wall clock.
  Non-goals: majority voting on verdicts (the coordinator weighs evidence, not votes) and members
  seeing each other inside a wave (blindness stays). When every model shares a blind spot a
  unanimous panel is confidently wrong; the remedy is evidence - findings say what was verified in
  code and what was inferred, and the coordinator checks them (R9) - not more votes.
- **R15 â€” Telemetry routing: companions chosen by their track record, with exploration (implemented
  in wave 26 with R14; see the CHANGELOG for what the draw and the score became).** The scoreboard (`codex-scoreboard.ps1`, the `-Rate` usefulness marks,
  reviewer x purpose) becomes the router's input. Selection is a weighted draw, not a fixed order: a
  reviewer's weight grows with its rated usefulness on this purpose - and on topic tags a brief
  carries (`-Topic concurrency,powershell`) - while a small exploration share keeps less-used or
  newly updated models in rotation (a new model id starts with a neutral prior; old marks decay).
  Availability comes first: the draw is only among entries the preflight, quota and peak rules
  allow. Pieces: `-Topic`, a routing record in the ledger (weights, the draw, why each member was
  picked), `codex-scoreboard.ps1 -By topic`. Measured by the share of findings the coordinator rates
  useful per consultation, before and after.
- **R16 â€” Companion roles (implemented in wave 26: `-Role`, `-Roles`, `templates/role-*.md`).** Besides a general review a companion can take one narrow role:
  edge-case hunter, security reviewer, test designer who proposes failing tests as text, docs
  checker. Expressed as brief templates and purpose presets; members stay read-only and the
  coordinator applies what survives verification.
- **A fourth seat (e.g. MiMo-V2.6)** only after a capped project-local evaluation (seeded
  historical defects plus clean controls at a fixed budget) on an officially supported route;
  leaderboard rank is not that evidence. Consider replacing a role before adding a reviewer.

- **R17 â€” Telemetry and complaints to the maintainer's intake, on by default (implemented in the 0.5.0 candidate, wave 28; the intake itself is not deployed yet - events wait in the local spool).** So
  that the bridge can be improved when someone the maintainer never hears from uses it, a run
  can report ONE anonymised event per consultation, and the operator can file a complaint, to
  the maintainer's intake (`https://xelth.com/T/v2/...`, the "T-hub" spec kept in that site's
  roadmap). ON by default (the maintainer's decision of 2026-09-26: an opt-in intake collects
  nothing); the README states that installing the plugin means accepting its terms, what is sent
  and what never is, and the one-line switch `CODEX_CONSULT_TELEMETRY=off` (or `-Telemetry off`
  per run); the SessionStart line and the dry run say whether it is on, and the first run after
  an install prints the notice once. The event, sent after
  the ledger commit from a local spool (`<codex home>/telemetry-spool/`, NDJSON, sent in the
  background with a 3 s timeout and retried on the next run, dropped after 7 days - never
  blocking a consultation): `app_id` (`codex-consult`, `c3` from 1.0.0), the plugin version, an
  instance id (`sha256(salt file + machine name)`), `event_type: consultation`, severity, and
  `details` = engine, provider label, model, purpose, outcome class (`usable`, `failed:<class>`),
  wall seconds, token counts, findings counts, structured or not, a format retry or not, panel
  size, PowerShell version, OS. NEVER: task names, prompts, briefs, paths, thread ids, finding
  texts, keys. `codex-consult.ps1 -Complain "<text>"` prints the exact payload (the text plus the
  last ledger entry's summary), asks for confirmation unless `-Yes`, sends it and prints the
  `public_ref` to quote. Tests with a local fake endpoint only (never the real intake in a
  harness). README "Telemetry (opt-in)" with the exact payload and the privacy statement.
  Non-goals: any identifying data, any send without the switch, any send that can slow or fail
  a run.
- **R18 â€” Member control: stall auto-cut, `-Kick`, per-entry timeouts (wave 26b; wave 26c: kick acknowledgement, the stall timer on bytes and suspended during tool calls; from live use on
  2026-09-27).** A coordinator watching a panel could not shorten one slow member: a reviewer that
  had stopped producing events held the panel for its whole budget (1800 s plus the 900 s
  continuation), and the only manual remedy was killing its process by hand. Pieces: (a) a stall
  detector - a member whose event stream has been silent for `-StallSec` (default 900; roster
  `stall_sec` per entry; 0 off) while its process lives is stopped like a timeout, with the same
  continuation turn and salvage, `bridge_outcome` `failed: stalled after N s without an event`;
  (b) `-Kick <nn>` for one member of a running panel (`-Kick -Id <id8> -Member <nn>` on a detached
  panel; a kick file the foreground parent polls otherwise): the member is stopped, its partial
  output salvaged, the member recorded `failed: stopped by the operator (-Kick)` (class `operator`),
  the panel goes on; (c) a roster entry's `timeout_sec` replacing the purpose default for that
  member (an explicit `-TimeoutSec` still wins for all). Non-goal: restarting a kicked member.
- **R19 â€” The coordinator's manual ships with the bridge (implemented in wave 27 with R13: the `coordinate` skill, the agent files, `-Explain`; the idle watchdog rule added in wave 27b).** The rules a
  coordinator needs to run consultations well - waves and briefs, a fresh worker per wave, reports
  as files, non-blocking waits (`-Detach`, background runs, a watchdog wake below the prompt-cache
  TTL that reads the worker's state file and messages or kicks it), context hygiene (the
  auto-compaction threshold, compaction at wave boundaries), never redoing a worker's work, the
  language rule, the live-member rule (no writes under the collab directory or the working tree
  while an agy or muse member runs) - live today in one operator's private CLAUDE.md. A plugin
  cannot ship a CLAUDE.md, so the manual becomes a skill (`coordinate`, host-neutral, English),
  the worker agent definitions ship in the plugin's `agents/` (the Codex host gets its
  counterparts from the R13 install script), and the SessionStart hook prints one pointer line
  beside the availability line. Reviewed with R13 in one design panel.
- **R20 â€” Machine-wide endpoint health (wave 26b; wave 26c: lock retries and the retry at the ledger commit).** Endpoint health lives in the ledgers of one
  repository, so two repositories consulting the same endpoint at once cannot see each other's
  bursts: on 2026-09-27 a BytePlus member of this repository's acceptance panel failed with 429
  after 2568 s while another repository's panels used the same endpoint. A small store under the
  codex home (`codex-consult-health.json`, path overridable by `CODEX_CONSULT_HEALTH`, written under
  a lock) records provider failures and usable replies per endpoint and the members running per
  endpoint (pid + start time liveness); every roster walk reads it beside the repository's ledgers,
  and the endpoint parallel limit counts running members of every repository. Absent or unreadable
  = today's behaviour.
- **R21 â€” The scoreboard says what is computed and what is asserted (candidate, from use on
  2026-09-28).** A rating is the judge's assertion; a finding verified with evidence is closer to a
  measurement. The scoreboard shows both in one score. A column for the evidence behind each
  number (verified findings with their evidence against ratings alone) lets a reader see how much
  of a reviewer's standing rests on checked work.
- **R22 â€” Reviewer child hygiene beyond the environment (candidate, from the live host checks of
  2026-09-29).** Wave 27 removes the coordinator's session markers from a reviewer's environment.
  Two things still reach a reviewer that it has no use for: the plugins, skills and hooks of the
  host the engine belongs to (after the plugin is installed on the Codex host, every `codex exec`
  reviewer sees the coordinator's skills), and the engine's multi-agent tools (one reviewer spent
  its run in `wait` calls with nobody to wait for and never read the brief). Reviewer children
  start with the coordinator's plugin switched off and without multi-agent tools, per engine, and
  the ledger records what was switched off.
- **R23 â€” Waiting without losing the cache (rule in wave 27b, description in wave 27d).** A
  coordinator with a large context never lets its prompt cache expire by oversight: a recurring
  wake while anything runs or is awaited (another session's window included), the boundary
  between refreshing the cache and compacting computed from the prices (README "Waiting: keep the
  prompt cache or compact"), compaction at wave boundaries and only while the cache is warm. Open:
  a host-independent way for the agent to compact its own context (on the host checked, the agent
  has none).

- **R24 â€” The public page computes reviewer usefulness from live telemetry (candidate, operator
  2026-09-30).** The page `/C3/` of the maintainer's site shows a hand-collected usefulness table (about 55
  consultations of 22-26 September) beside a live telemetry section. The bridge sends one more allowlisted
  event when the judge rates a consultation (`rating`: the vendor class, the model from the closed list, the
  purpose, `useful: yes | partly | no`, no text), as C3 already does; the site aggregates consultations and
  ratings per vendor class and model (n, usable rate, findings per consultation, blockers, mean wall seconds,
  ratings) over a window and renders the table from that, dated, with the hand-collected snapshot kept as the
  baseline. The site's half lives in the site's repository. **The bridge's half is implemented
  (2026-10-06):** `codex-findings.ps1 -Rate` spools one `rating` event (details `engine`,
  `provider`, `model`, `purpose`, `mark`, `age_days`, `bridge_version`, `os`, `ps_version`; the
  switch honoured; `-Telemetry on|off` for one rating) - README "Telemetry (on by default)",
  `harness-telemetry` RATE; `codex-telemetry.ps1 -BackfillRatings` sent the earlier marks once (0.5.1). **The site's half is live (2026-10-06):** `/C3/` renders the table from `GET /T/v2/public/usefulness?app_id=codex-consult&days=90`, the hand-collected snapshot folded below as the baseline. R24 done.

### Browser engine - web-chat reviewers through the user's own Chrome tab (OPERATOR DIRECTION 2026-10-14)

**Ask (operator, 2026-10-14):** many labs answer for free, or under a chat subscription the user already has, only in
the browser (Gemini web with a Pro plan -> gemini-3.8-flash; grok.com free questions; others). Add a bridge engine that
drives those web UIs through Chrome, so a roster can hold `browser :: gemini-web`, `browser :: grok` next to the CLI and
API engines. Per-site adapters must be user-extensible, rated by the same usefulness telemetry, and distributed through
that channel - the xelixir/9eck model: sandboxed WASM inserts, enabled per user, scored in the field.
**Boundary (operator):** this sits in a grey zone of the sites' terms, so it must NOT be our program: the bridge ships
the neutral frame (engine, adapter contract, sandbox, telemetry, catalogue format); site adapters are written, enabled
and run by users in their own browser sessions. We publish no adapter for a site whose terms forbid automation.

- **Prior art to reuse (same author):** C:/Users/Dmytro/gemini-mcp - a Chrome extension + local WebSocket relay that
  gives the free Gemini web app MCP tools; no API key, no cookies (the signed-in tab is the credential; the cookie/HTTP
  replay path was removed as fragile - PROTOCOL.md), DESIGN.md 'WebSocket message contract' / 'Security stance';
  C:/Users/Dmytro/xelth.rs - the Chrome extension 'DOM Heuristic Doctor' (retry loops, fuzzy selectors, status badge)
  bridging the Gemini web UI to a local Claude Code loop.
- **Shape.** Engine `browser` (C3 first - it already has engines codex/agy/muse/claude/http and the reviewer pack): C3
  <-> local WebSocket <-> Chrome extension <-> site adapter. The adapter implements one small contract - new_chat,
  send(text), await_answer() -> text, attach(file)?, limits() - against the site's DOM. Adapters are WASM modules run
  in the extension (browser WASM runtime; a strict host API: DOM query/click/type/read of the chat tab only, no cookies,
  no other tabs, no network), signed and listed in a catalogue; the user enables an adapter per site.
- **Read-only by construction.** A web reviewer has no repository tools, so it gets the reviewer pack (brief + periphery
  within a per-adapter token budget - free tiers are small); the reply is captured verbatim and goes through the same
  ledger/findings/rating path as every other engine. Nothing leaves the machine except the pack text typed into the
  user's own chat tab, by the user's own session, at a human cadence (rate limits per adapter; the user sees every turn).
- **Telemetry and distribution.** Every consultation row already carries engine/provider/model and the usefulness mark;
  add adapter_id/adapter_version/site. The usefulness site (/C3/) aggregates per adapter; adapters are fetched and
  updated through the same telemetry/usefulness channel (opt-in), with signatures - the xelixir WASM-shield rule
  (installed by the user, lands disabled, enabled explicitly) applies.
- **Order.** (1) extension + WS relay lifted from gemini-mcp into a C3 `browser` engine with the adapter contract and
  NO built-in adapter; (2) WASM host API + catalogue format + signing; (3) telemetry fields + /C3/ per-adapter table;
  (4) a reference adapter kept OUTSIDE the product (example repo / user-land) to prove the contract; (5) PowerShell
  plugin parity only if the host-invariance rule needs it (likely C3-only).
- **Status:** direction recorded 2026-10-14; a reviewer panel on the design/boundary is the next step; not scheduled.

## Tech debt observed in use (2026-09-26; scheduled as the "operator visibility" wave)

- **T1 - timeouts for big reviews.** A `-Purpose diff-review -Panel -PanelAll` run on a
  ~4,000-line commit range lost BOTH members to the 900 s default timeout (each killed at
  ~902 s), while the same reviewers had taken 585 s and 778 s on a framing brief that morning; an
  acceptance of a large wave later lost three of seven members at 1800 s. Nothing of a killed
  member's work survives: the reply file holds no prose and the event stream is not salvaged.
  Planned: (a) per-purpose default timeouts (diff-review, acceptance and core-contract above the
  900 s of a checkpoint), with `-TimeoutSec` still winning; (b) a preflight WARNING when the
  reviewed range is large for the timeout (lines changed in the range, files named by the
  brief), suggesting `-TimeoutSec` or a reading plan in the brief; (c) on a timeout kill, salvage
  the last agent message and reasoning text of the event stream into
  `<NN>-<engine>-<slug>.partial.md`, named in the ledger entry and the summary; (d) document
  rating a failed or timed-out member (`-Rate` is allowed; mark `no` only when the failure was
  the reviewer's, skip it when it was the bridge's or the plan's).
- **T2 - the providers view disagrees with the roster walk.** `codex-providers.ps1` showed a
  reviewer "available", LAST FAILURE "-" and "roster: would select" it, while every panel of the
  day skipped that same entry with "usage limit until <time>". The listing must reflect the same
  endpoint health the roster walk uses (the ledgers of the repository the command runs in), or
  say where its state comes from; otherwise the skill's advice "do not plan on an unavailable
  provider" cannot be followed from its output.
- **T3 - a quota failure without a reset time reads as available.** After two members of one
  plan failed with 429 (class quota, no reset time known), the SessionStart line and the
  listing still said the plan was available. A fresh quota failure without a reset must count as
  "out (limit hit <time>, reset unknown)" for a documented window (60 min), see also the
  companions design's addendum (what is out, per roster entry, one line).

- **T4 - the harnesses as an oracle for other implementations.** Every harness resolves the
  scripts it drives through a hard-coded relative path (`$scripts` near the top of each
  `tests/harness-*.ps1`), so a second implementation of the same CLI (the Rust C3) can run the
  ~750 assertions only by dropping shim files into a checkout. Planned (wave 25): an env override
  `CODEX_CONSULT_SCRIPTS_DIR` and a `-ScriptsDir` parameter on `run-all.ps1` and on each harness,
  read once at the top, defaulting to the checkout's `plugins/codex-consult/scripts`; the run-all
  summary names the directory it tested. No behaviour change without the override.

## Bridge features (earlier help-wanted list)

- **A bash port**, so macOS/Linux users need no `pwsh` at all.
- **A `UserPromptSubmit` hook injector**: inject the last Codex reply into the next turn, or
  detect an `@codex` trigger token and launch a consult. The hook budget is ~30 s by default,
  so a synchronous consult does not fit: inject stored context or fire detached.
- **The reverse direction**: a Codex-side tool that consults Claude.
- **An MCP server variant** with background jobs, so a long consult does not block the turn.
- **Tests on macOS** (Linux via WSL and PowerShell 7 are exercised by `tests/run-all.ps1`; macOS is not).
- ~~**`--output-schema` support** (the substrate for R3).~~ **Shipped in 0.2.0** as the
  substrate of R3 (structured findings).

Issues and PRs welcome for any of these.

## Transport: an in-tab extension relay (and why not cookies)

We do **not** call the model. The browser is the client; we are a passive
tool server. A Chrome content script lives inside the tab the user is
already logged into, reads the model's replies out of the DOM, relays them
to our local WebSocket server, and injects our results back into the input
box. Authentication is simply "the user's tab is open and logged in".

This is the approach the xelth.rs bridge has run in production for months.
It replaced an earlier, abandoned design:

- **Cookie replay (tried, abandoned).** The first design authenticated with
  the browser cookie pair (`__Secure-1PSID`, `__Secure-1PSIDTS`) and
  replayed Gemini's private HTTP API directly. It worked, but
  `__Secure-1PSIDTS` rotates every few minutes, so the session died
  constantly â€” every stale-token cycle needed a re-import, and the whole
  path rode an undocumented wire protocol that could break without notice.
  The reverse-engineered protocol notes are preserved in `PROTOCOL.md` for
  the historical record; that code is gone.
- **In-tab extension relay (what we run).** No cookies, no HTTP
  reverse-engineering, no token rotation. The user's live session *is* the
  auth. If the tab is logged in, it works; nothing to expire.

Residual risk, stated plainly: automated use of the consumer web app is
contrary to Google's terms â€” the program is a personal client for a
person's own account and must never be presented otherwise.

## Tool protocol: get past the guardrail, then stay robust

There is no function-calling API on the consumer web surface, so tool use
has to be negotiated in prose â€” and the consumer `gemini.google.com` model
carries a guardrail that refuses tool-calling framings outright. The design
here is the product of walking three framings, in order:

1. **` ```tool_code ` (refused).** The obvious move is to reuse the fenced
   `tool_code` / `tool_output` convention Gemini is trained on in
   Antigravity and the Gemini CLI. The web model refuses it: it treats
   `tool_code` as a sandbox it "does not have" and answers "that tool is
   not available in this environment". The same refusal fires for any
   framing that asserts the model *has tools* or is *connected to a
   harness that wants JSON back*.

2. **Human-operator `REQUEST:` / `RESULT:` (worked, but fragile).** Casting
   the far side as a *person* who looks things up slips past the guardrail:
   told "I'm your operator, ask me and I'll paste back what I find", the
   model emits `REQUEST: <name> <args>` and reads a pasted `RESULT:`. This
   shipped â€” but the social-role framing is brittle: the model periodically
   "remembers" it is an AI with no operator and stops cooperating.

3. **xelth-style delegation tags (what we run).** The xelth.rs browser
   bridge solved the identical problem and ran it in production for months:
   cast the model as a lead/architect that **delegates tasks to local
   worker agents**, emitted as custom XML-like blocks a relay executes and
   answers. The guardrail never fires on "hand a task to your helpers" the
   way it does on "call a tool". This is the battle-tested form, so it is
   the protocol:

   - The primer (served at `/api/primer`, pasted into a fresh chat by the
     user) lists the shim's MCP tools as Python-like signatures built from
     each tool's `inputSchema`, framed as what the local helpers can do.
   - The model delegates one operation per block:
     `<mcp_task id="t1" tool="mesh_nodes">{"argument": "value"}</mcp_task>`
     â€” a fresh sequential id per block, a JSON-object body (empty / `{}` for
     a no-argument call).
   - The parser scans the whole reply (not line by line, so fenced or
     inline-backtick-wrapped blocks are found), rejects unknown tools,
     placeholder-id examples (a real xelth incident: the primer's own
     example block dispatched with id `"..."`), placeholder argument
     values, and dedups repeats.
   - Results go back as the sibling tag, echoing the id so the model can
     pair them:
     `<mcp_result id="t1" tool="mesh_nodes" status="ok">{"data": â€¦}</mcp_result>`.

The tag is a deliberate, proven dialect â€” not the model's native format,
because the model's native format is exactly what the guardrail rejects.

## WebSocket message contract

The relay binds strictly to `127.0.0.1:4455` (override with
`GEMINI_MCP_WS_ADDR`). Every inbound **text** frame maps to exactly one
reply (or none):

| Inbound | Reply |
|---|---|
| `"ping"` | `"pong"` â€” the extension heartbeats every 15s to stop Chrome dropping an idle socket. |
| `{"type":"ext_log","level":..,"message":..}` | none; logged at the matching tracing level. |
| `{"type":"replay","id":".."}` | the cached response, or `<mcp_status â€¦ state="in_progress"/>` / `state="unknown"/>` â€” never re-executed. |
| text with dispatchable `<mcp_task>` blocks | one `<mcp_result>` per task, joined. Deduped by the first task id via the ledger. |
| text with an `<mcp_result` but no dispatchable task | `<mcp_status state="ignored_echo"/>` â€” our own result echoed back into the chat. |
| blocks that only produce rejections | one error `<mcp_result â€¦ status="error">` that teaches the correct syntax. |
| plain prose with no blocks | none. |

**Task ledger.** Dedup is by task id (ported from the xelth bridge): a new
id executes; an id in flight gets `in_progress`; a completed id gets its
cached response resent verbatim. The completed history is a FIFO capped at
50. This exists because the extension can re-dispatch the same block after
a reconnect or a DOM re-render â€” a bare "seen" set would swallow the retry
and hang the Gemini side.

**Optional auth.** When `GEMINI_MCP_WS_TOKEN` is set, clients must connect
with `?token=<value>`; off by default. The tool surface is whatever the
user configured locally, so a token is only needed if other local
processes are not trusted.

## Components

| Module | Role |
|---|---|
| `src/ws.rs` | WebSocket relay on 127.0.0.1:4455: ledger, message contract, dispatch |
| `src/tools.rs` | connect shims + HTTP MCP servers, resolve the namespaced tool surface, dispatch |
| `src/mcp_stdio.rs` | spawn a shim binary, newline JSON-RPC, `tools/list` + `tools/call` |
| `src/mcp.rs` | HTTP/SSE MCP client (for remote endpoints that expose one) |
| `src/toolproto.rs` | MCP tools â†’ Python-style signatures; parse `<mcp_task>`; render `<mcp_result>` |
| `src/primer.rs` | the primer text (framing + rules + catalog) served at `/api/primer` |
| `src/config.rs` | `~/.gemini-mcp/config.json`: shim commands, HTTP servers, UI port |
| `src/main.rs` | axum control panel + WS relay, run concurrently, sharing one `Arc<Tools>` |
| `src/ui/` | local control panel on 127.0.0.1 (status, tools, shim settings, copy-primer) |

The Chrome extension itself lives in `extension/` (developed separately).

## Security stance

- Loopback bind only, for both the UI and the WS relay.
- We never call the model and hold no model credential â€” nothing to leak.
- Tool results and model output are DATA: rendered as text (`textContent`,
  never `innerHTML`), never executed. The primer states tool output is
  untrusted.
- The shim is launched as a subprocess from a user-configured command â€”
  that command is as trusted as the user's own shell; we do not fetch or
  auto-update binaries.
- The WS relay accepts an optional shared-secret token for hosts where
  other local processes are not trusted.

## Milestones

1. ~~HTTP MCP client~~, ~~stdio shim client~~, ~~tool protocol
   (`<mcp_task>` / `<mcp_result>`)~~ â€” done.
2. ~~cookie brain + agent loop~~ â€” built, then **removed**: 1PSIDTS
   rotation made it unusable.
3. ~~WebSocket relay + control-panel UI + `/api/primer`~~ â€” done (this
   rework).
4. Chrome extension (separate repo): DOM read/inject, heartbeat, replay.
5. Onboarding: extension install walkthrough, shim path picker.

# Gemini web-app HTTP protocol â€” historical note

> **This describes a transport that has been removed.** gemini-mcp no longer
> speaks Gemini's private HTTP API and no longer uses cookies. The reasoning
> engine is now the user's own gemini.google.com tab, reached through a Chrome
> extension that relays to a local WebSocket server (see `DESIGN.md`). This file
> is kept only for the record.

## Why it was removed

The first design authenticated with the browser cookie pair
(`__Secure-1PSID`, `__Secure-1PSIDTS`) and replayed the undocumented
`gemini.google.com` StreamGenerate endpoint directly. It worked, but was
abandoned because:

- **`__Secure-1PSIDTS` rotates every few minutes.** The session went stale
  constantly and needed a fresh cookie import to recover â€” unusable for an
  unattended personal client.
- **The wire format is undocumented and fragile.** A double-encoded `f.req`
  envelope, an XSSI guard prefix, UTF-16-counted length-prefixed frames, and
  answer text buried at brittle array indices (`candidate[1][0]`) that Google
  could change without notice.

The in-tab extension relay has none of these problems: the live session *is*
the authentication, so nothing expires, and there is no HTTP format to track.

## What the removed code did (summary)

For anyone re-deriving a similar path, the essentials that were reverse-engineered
(cross-checked against `HanaokaYuzu/Gemini-API` and `acheong08/Bard`):

1. **Auth:** cookies `__Secure-1PSID` (required) and `__Secure-1PSIDTS`

## Quickstart

```bash
# Index a project
cargo run -- index --path ./src

# Index with fast mock embeddings (no GPU/API needed)
cargo run -- --embed-mode gemini index --path .

# Search the knowledge graph
cargo run -- search "hybrid search"
cargo run -- search "SurrealDB" --abstract-mode --max-kb 8

# Watch for changes and re-index
cargo run -- watch --path ./src

# Start the WebSocket bridge with background re-indexing
cargo run -- serve --watch ./src

# Start the full automation loop (Headless Chrome + Bridge + Claude)
cargo run -- swarm --watch .

# Login to Google first (interactive Chrome, one-time setup)
cargo run -- swarm --login
```

## Architecture

See [`.eck/ARCHITECTURE.md`](.eck/ARCHITECTURE.md) for the full system design.

```
Chrome Extension --> WS (port 4444) --> GLM Orchestrator --> Claude Code (-p) --> WS --> Chrome
                                    \-> GraphRAG (SurrealDB) for tool calls
```

## Requirements

- Rust toolchain (edition 2021)
- Chrome (for Swarm mode)
- Claude Code CLI (`claude`) installed and on PATH

item.text:
I have enough context. Note key facts:

1. EngineKind is a Rust enum (codex, agy, muse, claude, http) with a `capabilities()` table. A `browser` engine needs PromptDelivery that isn't stdin/file — the enum has Stdin, StdinNdjsonLine, PromptFile. No "browser" delivery. So the design must extend `PromptDelivery` / serialized engine kind, and the plugin's `$script:Engines` table. Also `EngineKind` serde rename_all lowercase means `browser` is a new variant. Wire compat with PowerShell plugin (roster entries). This is a real framing gap: the brief/ROADMAP does not mention the engine-kind enum, capability table, or the roster/catalogue format used by `codex-providers.ps1`. Adding `browser` is a contract change to the engine surface shared with the PowerShell plugin — a versioning question.

2. The reply ingestion: engines return validated v1 structured reply. For http engine, continuation = replay. For browser engine, continuation would be the site's thread (trusted?) or stateless resend. The `ConversationTrust` concept exists — good precedent for Q4.

3. The pack budget exists (tokens = chars/4), redaction exists. Per-adapter pack budget: budget is per-pack `-Budget`, not per-engine; free tiers small → per-adapter default budget required.

4. Ids/ledger/telemetry: telemetry module exists. The ROADMAP says add adapter_id/adapter_version/site to consultation rows.

5. Findings: how would a browser reply that is prose-only (no JSON schema) be handled? Web chat models can't do structured output reliably — no output-schema transport. Grok/Gemini web can be prompted but JSON is unreliable. This is a major framing gap: the brief assumes "verbatim reply → usual ledger/findings/rating path", but the findings path needs structured JSON. The `http` engine has PromptOnly schema transport, so there's precedent, but with a web UI there's no retry-with-schema and no error signalling; also the "verbatim reply" is DOM-scraped and may be truncated by the site's own rendering (Gemini virtualizes long chats; also copy/selection). Key risk: DOM scrape is lossy — markdown artifacts, KaTeX, code fences, and the reply may be summarized. That's a real quality/robustness issue.

6. The boundary question: precedents — userscript managers (Tampermonkey/Greasemonkey: ship no scripts, user installs), browser extensions (Chrome Web Store policy: single purpose, user data), Selenium/Playwright (ship no site drivers, no stealth), OpenInterpreter, LangChain browser tools, "bring your own session" products (e.g., v0? no). Key precedents: 
- Tampermonkey/Greasemonkey/Violentmonkey: host ships no userscripts; a catalogue (openuserjs.org) lists user-authored scripts with hashes; no legal responsibility taken on.
- Browser extensions that drive sites: "no built-in selectors" is degraded by auto-updating selectors (e.g., some extensions ship selectors and break ToS). Counter-precedent: Microsoft's "Playwright" ships nothing site-specific; Selenium "no stealth".
- Precedent for the "neutral frame" argument being weak: Shipping a relay + adapter contract + "browser engine" still constitutes a tool "designed to automate" — Liable? The DMCA §1201 anti-circumvention doesn't apply (no circumvent), but CFAA "exceeds authorized access" is generally about servers; the user's own credentialed session is the strongest defense (hiQ v. LinkedIn; Meta v. Bright Data 2024 — scraping logged-in as yourself, terms breach not CFAA). Also, the site's ToS binds the *user* who accepted it, not the tool author — but tortious interference / "designed to breach" claims (e.g., Meta v. Bright Data rejected; X Corp v. Bright Data rejected). Practically: product name should not be site-specific, no default enabled, no bundled adapter, no docs that say "how to use on gemini.google.com" beyond a contract example in a separate repo. The catalogue must be a pointer list — id, site domain, adapter hash, version, publisher key — and must NOT host code (only pointer to the user's repo) OR, if it lists, be a pure hash/name directory with a signed pointer. Actually, "the product hosting adapter code it did not author" — Q5 asks the shape. Answer: catalogue = signed manifests (JSON) with id/site/semver/hash/signer/fetch URL; the fetch is user-initiated from a URL the user pastes; the bridge never bundles.

Also important: the Chrome extension itself must not contain per-site DOM code — which means the extension's manifest permissions should be minimal and dynamically requested per site (optional_host_permissions), granted by the user per site. That's a concrete boundary requirement the brief doesn't mention: `host_permissions` must not enumerate sites; use `optional_host_permissions` + `chrome.permissions.request` at enable time. If the extension lists gemini.google.com in the manifest, the product itself names the site → boundary hole.

Another boundary hole: the extension's name/description/store listing. Chrome Web Store prohibits "automation" and requires single purpose; also the Web Store review would flag. And a key structural issue: Chrome Web Store policy forbids remotely-hosted code and eval — so WASM adapters must be bundled or... wait: MV3 forbids remotely hosted code executed via eval, but data fetched and executed is banned; WASM fetched at runtime = remotely hosted code? Chrome's policy: "Remotely hosted code" includes WebAssembly? The policy says code must be packaged inside the extension; WASM fetched from a server and instantiated is remotely hosted code (WebAssembly.instantiateStreaming on fetched bytes counts as remote code execution banned under MV3 policy). This is a *major* technical finding: the ROADMAP's "adapters fetched and updated through the telemetry channel" directly conflicts with MV3's remotely-hosted-code policy — that could get the extension delisted (which is the product's distribution channel!). Two options: (a) distribute adapters out-of-band (user downloads a .wasm and places/loads it via a file picker — still "code executed", MV3 bans only *remote* code loaded at runtime... local user-provided file is a grey area but considered user-supplied), (b) distribute the host as a locally-loaded unpacked extension (no Web Store) — then MV3 policy is not enforced. Given the product already lives in a grey zone, the store is risky anyway. But the brief must decide: Web Store or sideload. The brief/ROADMAP says nothing about distribution of the *extension itself*. That's a real framing gap with a big consequence (auto-update, MV3 policy, sideload warnings in Chrome).

Also: Chrome's new Manifest V3 "Developer mode" extension warnings; Chrome may disable unpacked extensions. And the signature requirement: signatures only matter if there's a trust root; who signs? The user's own key? A project key would make the project an adapter distributor by proxy (counter to boundary). So signing must be publisher keys + a user-pinned trust set (TOFU), not a project CA. That's an important correction to "signatures → user-installed, lands disabled".

Also anti-detection: the brief asks "no headless, no CAPTCHA handling, hard stop on anti-automation signal". But running in the *user's* Chrome with a content script *is* detectable: `navigator.webdriver` no, but extension-injected DOM artifacts, event `isTrusted:false` for synthetic clicks/dispatch, React synthetic events. Sites detect automation via isTrusted on input events — synthetic `element.click()` and value-setting + `input` event produce untrusted events; Gemini/Grok can flag. Concrete requirement: adapter host API should use CDP-level Input events (Input.dispatchKeyEvent via chrome.debugger) rather than JS synthetic events, so events are trusted... but chrome.debugger displays the "being debugged" infobar → visible. So a real design fork: `chrome.debugger` (trusted events, visible infobar, matches "user sees every turn") vs content-script DOM events (invisible, untrusted). This is *the* central technical trade the brief does not mention. Also `chrome.debugger` gives access to network but also lets you read cookies → conflicts with "no cookies". Host API should be debugger-scoped, not the raw debugger.

Also, Grok.com free tier — grok.com free requires login now, and x.com has automation rules. Gemini web ToS: Google's ToS prohibits "automated queries" — the gemini-mcp repo already states "automated use of the consumer web app is contrary to Google's terms". So the operator's claim "we ship no adapter for a site whose terms forbid automation" implies we ship nothing at all, since both named sites forbid it — the only compliant artefact is the frame + a non-site-specific contract, and even the *engine* is arguably an automation tool. Point out: the boundary as stated is only credible if the product (a) never names a site, (b) has no site list in the catalogue *shipped* with the product, and (c) the reference adapter lives in a separate repo/site. Also the "product" and the "company" are the same in practice; the mitigation is the licence/README stance + no default enabled — the same stance gemini-mcp already takes. Recommend making the boundary a *documented refusal policy* (like a "no-adapter policy") rather than assuming the frame is neutral.

Also: DPA/ToS for the free web UI being "the credential" — the account is the user's; automating it may violate Gemini's ToS and Grok's, and could get the *user's account* banned, not just the product delisted. That is a real risk users must be warned about, and the product should surface it before enabling an adapter. The brief says the operator wants the company outside the grey area but does not mention the *user's account* exposure. That's a major framing omission (the mitigation: a mandatory consent gate with the text naming the risk, per adapter, not global).

Q3 additionally: what else? — (a) never auto-retry on a 429/site warning; (b) no unattended scheduling (no cron) — every turn requires a foreground user presence; (c) no more than N turns/hour and a random jitter min interval; (d) no persistence of site session/profile in the extension storage (no cookie reading); (e) no "keep-alive" pings that look like a bot; (f) hard-stop and *lock the adapter* on any anti-automation signal (a captcha element, a "verify you're human", a "you've hit your limit" — retire adapter version + drop the rating); (g) don't defeat virtualization — read only visible/rendered; (h) don't send the same prompt to many sites in parallel (correlated abuse footprint) — sequential, one tab at a time; (i) never alter the site's own settings; (j) no bypass of the free-tier question limits; (k) the "no CAPTCHA" must also mean "no auto-clicking a consent dialog that looks like a CAPTCHA".

Q4: reviewer quality. Concrete: pack budget per adapter should default to something like 4–8k tokens for free tiers (Gemini free ~32k context, but web-UI output and reliability degrade; grok free smaller) — but more importantly, the *pack is read-only* and web models lack repo tools → they cannot verify; mark them `read-only` reviewer class. Weighting: the router/panel existing scores — `scoreboard`/`usefulness` — should start the browser engine at the lowest band, and only raise it after ≥N rated consults with the same usefulness sampling. Also: structured reply reliability — the web chat cannot honour `--output-schema`; so a "PromptOnly" transport needs a repair step: the bridge should parse JSON; on failure, ask once for "resend as JSON only" (one repair turn) then, if still failing, store reply_markdown only and record `findings_unavailable`. Threads: prefer the site's own conversation for a multi-turn consultation *only* when the site's thread is stable and the adapter can name the conversation; otherwise stateless re-send (idempotent, replayable). The `http` engine precedent (continuation = replay) should be the default; the C3 `ConversationTrust` type is where to encode "site thread is not resumable across sessions/windows".

Q2 minimal adapter contract: current contract `new_chat / send(text) / await_answer() -> text / attach?(file) / limits()` is too weak in three ways:
- no identity/versioning in the contract (needs `id`, `site`, `version`, `dom_signature`/`contract_version`)
- `await_answer` needs to distinguish "streaming in progress" from "done" and to report the *turn boundary*; needs `wait_for_completion(timeout) -> {text, stopped, artifacts?}` and a `turns()`/`last_answer_is_final` notion; also needs `status()` for logged-out / rate-limited / captcha / updated-DOM detection
- no `capabilities()`/`limits()` semantics: `limits()` must express max input tokens, max turns, cooldown between turns, and whether a *thread* is continuable
- missing: `probe()`/health for the adapter (is the chat UI reachable / did the DOM change). Otherwise there's no way to detect churn and retire an adapter automatically — that's the whole point of the "rated and retired" plan.
- `attach(file)` is a problem: uploading a file into a web chat means the extension reads a local file and injects it — that crosses the "no repository tools" line and adds exfiltration surface (the pack would go as an attachment). Recommend: drop `attach` in v1; pack is typed text only. Also note that in the free tiers attachments often change the terms/quota.
- The contract must be *pull*: the adapter must never be handed a transcript to post; the host posts text the user can see. And the reply must be returned as text + a structured "ended" marker, and the host must cap reply length (sites truncate long code blocks on copy → verify the reply end marker).

Generic "textarea + answer container" site: `send` needs a way to choose the right textarea and the right "send" control (button or Enter), and `await_answer` needs a container selector + "generating" indicator. So the contract should be declarative-first (a selector map + a few verb hooks) rather than pure code where possible — declarative (JSON) is easier to sign, review, and sandbox, and can't exfiltrate. Strong recommendation: **two tiers** — a declarative JSON adapter (selectors + timing, no code) shipped as data, and a WASM escape hatch only for sites the declarative form can't cover. That's the biggest framing addition: the brief jumps straight to WASM without considering that most DOM adapters are declarative.

Also: WASM sandbox — WASM in a content script can be *imported* from JS; the JS glue is the actual trust boundary, not WASM. WASM modules cannot touch the DOM; they must call host imports; the *host* (extension JS) must implement DOM access, so the sandbox is only as good as the host API. Also, a content-script WASM instance can still exfiltrate via the host API only if the host API has a fetch/network verb — so the host API must have no network verb. And "no other tabs" — a content script is per-tab, but the extension's background can reach other tabs; the host API boundary must be enforced in the background, not the adapter. Additionally, WASM adapters could be used to obfuscate malicious behaviour (hide a network call behind a host import they trick) → the signing + review story must include "who reviews adapter code" — the project should NOT review/vouch; hence the catalogue is a directory, not an endorsement, and the hash is the identity.

Also important: the *extension* is the trust root. Once a user installs a browser engine extension with `scripting` + `tabs` + host permissions, the extension itself is a credential-adjacent agent. The security stance must include: extension ID pinned, no remote config that changes behaviour (a remote "kill switch" is itself remote code by proxy), update channel signed, and the WS relay authenticated (gemini-mcp's optional token should be mandatory in the product, plus origin checks, since the browser connects to loopback WS and any local process can talk to it → a rogue local process can inject prompts into the user's chat and read replies; the gemini-mcp stance has this as "off by default").

Also: the relay must authenticate the *extension* (not just any client) — the local WS is reachable from any page via ws://127.0.0.1 (websites can connect to localhost!). Chrome blocks mixed content but not plain ws to loopback from https pages? Actually ws:// from https page = mixed content blocked, but many browsers still allow loopback exceptions... Chrome allows ws://localhost from https? Chrome blocks mixed content but has an exception for localhost/127.0.0.1. Yes — Chrome's mixed-content policy treats http://127.0.0.1 as "potentially trustworthy", so a webpage CAN open ws://127.0.0.1:4455. So any website could connect to the relay if it knows the port → must require a token and validate Origin, and the token must be generated per run and given to the extension. That's a concrete blocker-level security requirement that the ROADMAP's "lifted from gemini-mcp" would inherit UNTOKENED by default. Good finding.

Q6: order of work / not to build. Recommend reordering: (0) write the boundary/refusal policy + the threat model + the manual, un-automated feasibility spike (can a human-shaped content script reliably drive one site and be undetected-plausible?) — because if the spike shows the site flags it in a day, the whole engine is dead. Then (1) declarative adapter schema + host API + relay with auth, (2) a user-land reference adapter in a separate repo, (3) telemetry fields, (4) WASM. Not build: no adapter for any site in this repo; no bundled catalogue with named sites; no CAPTCHA-solving or stealth/anti-fingerprinting; no headless; no file attachments; no scheduling/cron; no multi-tab parallel fan-out; no proxy rotation; no "warm-up" prompt to defeat detection; no PowerShell-parity; no Web Store publication if the adapter fetch model conflicts with MV3 (or accept sideloading).

What I'd need to know to choose between options (the brief asks "say what you would need to know"):
- Extension distribution channel (Web Store vs sideload) — determines MV3 remote-code legality and auto-update.
- Is the user willing to see a Chrome "debugger attached" infobar (chrome.debugger availability) → trusted events vs untrusted.
- Which sites are actually on the table and whether the user accepts the account-ban risk in writing.
- Does the host have to be C3/Rust, or can it be the plugin (host parity rule)? 
- Budget/quota per site and whether "the user sees every turn" can be enforced technically (foreground requirement).
- Whether the reply must be structured findings or prose-only is acceptable.
- Media/attachment support needed at all.

Now, the "framing review" purpose: I should surface unlisted options and challenge framing. Unlisted options:
- Option 0: don't build the engine; use the free web UI manually, paste the brief, paste the reply back into the bridge (a `-Engine manual`/`--reply-from-file` path) — an enormous fraction of the value at ~0 boundary risk. The brief doesn't list "manual relay" or "share-a-link" options at all. This is the strongest framing challenge: the bridge already supports a reviewer pack and a reply file; an `import-reply` path plus a "copy pack to clipboard / read reply from clipboard" command is 100% compliant and delivers web-chat reviewers today. Also consider the "user pastes the pack into the site and pastes the reply into the bridge" = human-in-the-loop browser engine.
- Option A: extension drives the tab (brief's option).
- Option B: the user's own *manual* browser + a clipboard bridge.
- Option C: an MCP/CLI path that the site itself offers (Gemini CLI free tier with Google account? Gemini CLI OAuth free tier = 1000 req/day — that's a *sanctioned* API-ish path with no browser automation at all! This is a big unlisted option: gemini-cli / Codex-style CLIs with subscription auth). Also: gemini-3.8-flash via "Gemini Code Assist"/Antigravity CLI (already the agy engine!) — the user already has an agy engine for Google models. So the real gap is grok, which has an API but no free API plan... There's also Grok's x.com. So Q: is the browser engine needed for Gemini at all, given `agy`? Push back on the premise: Gemini web with a Pro plan ≈ agy/Gemini CLI with the same account; the *only* genuinely new capability is sites with no CLI/API (grok.com free). So the engine's scope should be reduced to "generic web-chat sites" and the Gemini case should be re-examined (does the user's Pro plan not already cover the Gemini CLI? Gemini CLI free tier exists; Antigravity is wired). Excellent framing challenge.
- Option D: use the site's own "share conversation" or export, i.e., read-only scraping rather than driving (no sending at all — the user sends; the extension only reads the answer). Splitting send/read moves the automation from "bot sends" to "user sends, tool reads", which is far more defensible. This is a genuinely unlisted middle option and probably the best boundary posture: the *human* triggers the send (or presses Enter), the extension only extracts the answer to the ledger. The brief's Q3 "user sees every turn" hints at it but the contract assumes `send`.

Great, those are strong framing contributions.

Now findings. I need concrete defects/risks with locations (repo-relative paths in this repo — the brief, ROADMAP.md). Since findings must reference paths relative to the repository root (claude-codex-consult), I'll use `.collab/browser-engine-2026-10-14/handoffs/01-fable-browser-engine-framing.md` and `ROADMAP.md:371` etc.

Also: `-SchemaTransport` exists as a CLI arg. So a browser engine's schema transport must be `PromptOnly`, and the existing arg validation may reject new engines. Good detail.

## Framing: what the brief assumes
Three options it does not list.

**O-A Manual relay (near-zero risk, most value today).** C3 already builds a reviewer pack and ingests a reply file. Add `--reply-from <file>` (or clipboard) and a `pack --clipboard` command: the coordinator pastes the pack into the web chat by hand, pastes the reply back. 100% terms-neutral, no extension, no adapter, works for every site including ones with no adapter. The brief never considers that a human is already in the loop.

**O-B Read-only extraction (the defensible middle).** The user types/presses Enter in their own tab; the extension only *reads* the finished answer into the ledger and marks it. This shifts the product from "automates the site" to "reads a page the user is looking at", the weakest possible automation claim, and it still earns most of the telemetry/usefulness value. Only `await_answer`+DOM read is needed; `send`/`new_chat`/`attach` disappear. The brief's contract assumes send.

**O-C Sanctioned non-browser routes.** Gemini web with a Pro plan is not the only path to Google models — `agy` (Antigravity) already covers that account, and `gemini-cli` free OAuth tier exists.
